power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P < 2.1 ", "P = 0.336", "P = 0.336"), Sentence = c("Steiger directionality analyses supported the hypothesized direction from GrimAge AA to each clinical outcome (all Steiger P < 2.1 × 10¹).", "The association between 2-HF exposure and GGT was significantly mediated through GrimAge AA (ACME = 0.019, P = 0.0072), whereas the direct effect was not statistically significant (ADE = 0.024, P = 0.336).", "For 2-HF, the estimated average causal mediation effect was 0.019 (P = 0.0072), whereas the average direct effect was 0.024 (P = 0.336)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. • PAH biomarkers 2-HF and 2-NAP were key contributors to the exposure mixture.
• GrimAge acceleration was positively associated with WBC and GGT.
• GrimAge acceleration mediated environmental exposure-GGT associations.
• GrimAge showed suggestive links to diabetic nephropathy and osteoporosis.

Mediation analyses identified significant indirect effects through GrimAge acceleration for the associations of 2-HF, 2-NAP, bCd, and MHA with GGT.
Exploratory disease analyses further suggested potential associations with diabetic nephropathy and osteoporosis, together with an inverse association with cardiac valvular disease.

text.text: However, these relationships have largely been investigated separately, and relatively little is known about how exposure-related alterations in epigenetic aging relate to physiological and clinical changes within the same population.
Evidence also remains limited for some environmental chemicals, including VOC metabolites, in relation to DNA methylation-based aging measures.

Integrating environmental exposures, epigenetic aging, and health-related phenotypes within a single cohort may therefore provide a more comprehensive understanding of the potential biological pathways linking environmental exposures to adverse health outcomes.
The FROM cohort provides an opportunity to address these gaps in older adults residing in environmentally vulnerable areas.

Previous analyses of this cohort have identified heavy metal-associated multi-omic alterations and plasma proteomic profiles implicating immune, lipid, and oxidative-stress pathways (Heo et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Previous analyses of this cohort have identified heavy metal-associated multi-omic alterations and plasma proteomic profiles implicating immune, lipid, and oxidative-stress pathways <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Heo et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Kim et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, we evaluated associations of 13 environmental exposure biomarkers, including heavy metals, PAHs, and VOCs, with multiple epigenetic aging measures and additionally assessed the effects of combined exposures.

We further examined associations between epigenetic aging and clinical traits and evaluated the potential mediating role of epigenetic aging in the relationships between environmental exposures and clinical alterations.

Finally, we used Mendelian randomization (MR) based on East Asian genetic instruments to investigate potential causal relationships between epigenetic aging and clinical traits and extended these analyses to metabolic and age-related disease outcomes in Biobank Japan (BBJ) (Ishigaki et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Finally, we used Mendelian randomization (MR) based on East Asian genetic instruments to investigate potential causal relationships between epigenetic aging and clinical traits and extended these analyses to metabolic and age-related disease outcomes in Biobank Japan (BBJ) <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Ishigaki et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these analyses provide an integrated framework for examining potential links among environmental chemical exposures, epigenetic aging, clinical alterations, and age-related diseases.

text.text: In this community-based study of 666 older adults, including 553 residents of environmentally vulnerable areas and 113 controls, environmental exposure was associated with accelerated epigenetic aging and downstream physiological alterations.
Four findings were central.
First, among seven epigenetic aging measures, GrimAge AA showed the most consistent signal across both the exposed-versus-control comparison and biomarker-based analyses.
Second, PAH biomarkers, particularly 2-HF and 2-NAP, emerged as reproducible correlates of GrimAge AA across individual-and mixture-exposure models.

Third, GrimAge AA was associated with WBC, GGT, and LDL, but MR provided nominal support for a directional effect only for GGT; mediation analyses further identified indirect associations of 2-HF, 2-NAP, bCd, and MHA with GGT through GrimAge AA that remained significant after FDR correction.
Finally, exploratory disease MR suggested potential associations with diabetic nephropathy, osteoporosis, and cardiac valvular disease at FDR < 0.10.
text.formatted: Finally, exploratory disease MR suggested potential associations with diabetic nephropathy, osteoporosis, and cardiac valvular disease at FDR < 0.10.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that pollutant-associated GrimAge AA may reflect physiologically relevant biological alterations.
The specificity of the exposure signal to GrimAge is biologically informative.
In the regional comparison, Hannum AA and DunedinPACE were nominally significant, whereas epiTOC remained significant after FDR correction but was higher in controls.
In quantitative exposure models, only GrimAge AA retained associations after FDR correction, specifically with bCd, 2-NAP, 2-HF, and MHA.

First-generation clocks such as Horvath and Hannum were optimized primarily to predict chronological age, whereas GrimAge was trained to predict mortality using DNAm surrogates of smoking pack-years and mortality-related plasma proteins (Hannum et al., 2013; Horvath, 2013; Lu et al., 2019).

The opposite-direction epiTOC finding further suggests that mitotic age and mortality-related biological age represent distinct aging domains.
This interpretation is consistent with previous environmental epigenetic-aging studies.

The PAH findings were particularly consistent across analytical approaches.
In single-pollutant models, 2-HF showed a strong association with GrimAge AA (β = 0.491, P = 1.22 × 10 -14 ), which was observed in both men and women without evidence of sex interaction.
Qgcomp estimated a positive joint mixture effect, with positive weights for MHA, 2-HF, 2-NAP, and 1-HPH, while BKMR assigned posterior inclusion probabilities of 1.000 to both 2-HF and 2-NAP.
Their convergence across conventional regression, qgcomp, and BKMR therefore identifies 2-HF and 2-NAP as prominent contributors to the observed exposure signal.

Because these urinary metabolites reflect exposure to fluorene, naphthalene, and correlated combustion sources, however, the findings are more appropriately interpreted as markers of PAH-related exposure rather than evidence of toxicity from the measured metabolites themselves.
Several mechanisms may connect PAH exposure with GrimAge AA.

Parent PAHs can activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and induce CYP1A1 and CYP1B1, while metabolic activation generates electrophilic intermediates and o-quinones capable of forming DNA adducts and generating reactive oxygen species, DNA-strand breaks, and oxidative DNA damage (Endo et al., 2008; Park et al., 2005; Park et al., 2009; Xue & Warshawsky, 2005).

text.text: Shared mechanisms-including reactive metabolite formation, glutathione consumption, oxidative stress, and inflammatory signaling-could therefore explain why chemically distinct biomarkers converged on GrimAge AA and GGT.
At the same time, the short half-lives and source nonspecificity of several urinary metabolites require caution when assigning effects to individual parent compounds.
The clinical-trait analyses support the biological and clinical relevance of GrimAge AA beyond its role as a methylation-derived computational score.
GrimAge AA was positively associated with WBC and GGT and inversely associated with LDL after FDR correction.
The WBC association is compatible with systemic inflammatory or immune-cell activation, one of the pathways through which PAHs and metals may affect aging.

By contrast, the inverse LDL association was not supported by MR and may reflect lipidlowering treatment, comorbidity, nutrition, frailty, or survival-related selection in this older population; it should not be interpreted as a protective effect of accelerated aging.
Similarly, the observational association with WBC was not supported by MR.
GGT was therefore the most coherent downstream phenotype because it was supported by both the observational association and the MR analysis.
GGT provides a biologically plausible link between pollutant exposure and GrimAge-associated physiological dysregulation.

Beyond its conventional role as a hepatobiliary marker, GGT participates in extracellular glutathione metabolism and may increase in response to oxidative stress (Lee et al., 2004; Zhang & Forman, 2009).

text.text: The mediation results provide the most direct synthesis of these findings.
Significant indirect effects were observed for 2-HF, 2-NAP, bCd, and MHA in relation to GGT through GrimAge AA.
For 2-HF, the estimated average causal mediation effect was 0.019 (P = 0.0072), whereas the average direct effect was 0.024 (P = 0.336).

This pattern is compatible with a pathway in which repeated toxicant-related oxidative and inflammatory stress becomes embedded in a mortality-related DNAm signature, which then tracks or contributes to a glutathione-dependent hepatometabolic response reflected by GGT.
The result is strongest for 2-HF and 2-NAP because both were supported in the individual and mixture analyses, and because independent studies have linked them to GGT or related liver outcomes.
Importantly, a nonsignificant direct effect is not proof of complete mediation, and GrimAge should not be treated as a single molecular effector.
It is more plausibly an integrative record of smokinglike exposure, inflammation, protein regulation, and cumulative organ stress.
Moreover, the MR result supports the direction from GrimAge AA to GGT but does not validate the exposure-to-GrimAge portion of the mediation model.
Accordingly, the pathway should be interpreted as biologically coherent and hypothesis-generating rather than as definitive temporal causation.
Exploratory disease MR provided additional, although suggestive, evidence of clinical relevance.

Among 38 outcomes, diabetic nephropathy (β = 0.1812, P = 0.0025), osteoporosis (β = 0.0282, P = 0.0054), and cardiac valvular disease (β = -0.0545, P = 0.0074) showed suggestive associations with GrimAge AA at FDR < 0.10, although none met FDR < 0.05.

This study has several notable strengths.
First, it evaluated seven epigenetic aging measures that capture distinct dimensions of biological aging, allowing the relative specificity of the GrimAge signal to be assessed rather than assumed.
Second, the exposure findings were examined at complementary levels: regional exposure-group comparisons, individual biomarker associations, and multi-pollutant mixture models.

The concordance of results across multivariable regression, quantile g-computation, and BKMR-particularly for 2-HF and 2-NAP-strengthens confidence that these findings were not driven by a single modeling approach.

Third, the integration of clinical-trait analyses, mediation analyses, and Mendelian randomization extended the investigation beyond exposure-DNAm associations to evaluate their potential physiological and disease relevance.

Finally, the focus on older Korean adults residing in environmentally vulnerable areas addresses a population in which cumulative exposure burdens and susceptibility to aging-related effects may be especially relevant.
Several limitations should be considered.

First, exposure biomarkers, DNAm, and clinical measurements were largely assessed cross-sectionally, limiting temporal and causal interpretation, while single urine measurements may not adequately represent usual exposure to rapidly cleared PAHs and VOCs.

Second, residual confounding by smoking, second-hand smoke, alcohol use, diet, medication, occupation, socioeconomic conditions, and pre-existing disease remains possible; this is particularly relevant because GrimAge incorporates a DNAm smoking surrogate.
Third, the exposed group was older than controls, and residual age-related differences may remain despite the use of age-acceleration measures and covariate adjustment.
In addition, the relatively small control group (n = 113) limited the statistical power of the regional comparisons.

Fourth, although multiple epigenetic aging measures were evaluated, more recently developed measures, such as GrimAge2 and PCGrimAge, were not included, which may limit the comprehensiveness of our assessment of exposurerelated epigenetic aging.
Fifth, mediation analysis relies on strong no-unmeasuredconfounding assumptions that cannot be verified in this observational setting.
Sixth, DNA methylation was measured using two EPIC array versions, and although batch effects were corrected, residual array-related variation cannot be fully ruled out.

Finally, although we conducted sensitivity analyses to assess instrument strength, heterogeneity, and potential horizontal pleiotropy, the genetic instruments for GrimAge AA were derived from relatively small GWAS (n = 666 for the clinical-trait MR and n = 1,892 for the disease MR) using a relaxed significance threshold (P < 5 × 10).

In the clinical-trait MR analyses, the nominal association observed for GGT did not remain significant after correction for multiple testing across the three clinical outcomes.
Similarly, the disease MR findings achieved only suggestive significance at FDR < 0.10.

text.text: Differences in ancestry, phenotype definitions, and genetic architecture may further limit transportability, underscoring the need for independent replication.
This study indicates that environmental pollutant exposure-most consistently PAH exposure indexed by 2-HF and 2-NAP-is associated with accelerated mortality-related epigenetic aging.

GrimAge was the only aging measure that showed a coherent adverseexposure signal across regional and biomarker-based analyses, and its associations with GGT, mediation of several pollutant-GGT relationships, and suggestive MR links to diabetic nephropathy and osteoporosis support biological and clinical relevance.

These results support a broader framework linking environmental pollutants to accelerated epigenetic aging and, in turn, to adverse physiological change, with GGT serving as one downstream redoxhepatometabolic indicator rather than a terminal endpoint.

Longitudinal studies with repeated exposure measurements, serial DNAm profiling, component-level GrimAge analyses, and independently replicated genetic instruments are needed to determine whether reducing PAH and co-pollutant exposure can slow biological aging and lessen aging-related disease risk.
